title: Closest Common Org Group
statement:
Given a company organization hierarchy where groups form a rooted tree and each employee belongs to one or more groups, find the **closest (deepest) common group** that contains every employee in a target list.

Implement `closestCommonGroup(String[][] groupLinks, String[][] memberships, String[] targetEmployees)`:
- `groupLinks[i] = [parentGroup, childGroup]` defines a parent-to-child group edge in the org tree (one single root group has no parent).
- `memberships[j] = [groupName, employeeName]` assigns `employeeName` directly to `groupName`. An employee belongs to `groupName` and all of its ancestor groups.
- `targetEmployees` is a non-empty array of employee names to cover.
- Return the name of the deepest group (maximum distance from the root) that contains all distinct employees in `targetEmployees`. If an employee belongs to multiple groups, covering that employee requires being an ancestor of (or equal to) **at least one** of their groups.
- Return `null` if any target employee does not exist in `memberships` or if no common group exists.

Contract
- Group names are distinct non-empty strings forming a valid rooted tree (or a single group when `groupLinks` is empty and all memberships share one group).
- `targetEmployees` may contain duplicates; treat it as a set of distinct target employees.
- If multiple deepest groups tie (which can happen when an employee belongs to multiple groups), return the lexicographically smallest group name.

Examples
- Tree `Company -> Eng, HR`; `Eng -> Backend, Frontend`; Alice in `Backend`, Bob in `Frontend`, Carol in `HR`: closest common group for `[Alice, Bob]` is `Eng`; for `[Alice, Carol]` is `Company`.
- Same group: Alice and Dave both in `Backend` -> `Backend`.
- Multi-group employee: Eve in `Backend` and `HR`, Carol in `HR` -> `[Eve, Carol]` is `HR`.

examples.input: Company>Eng, Company>HR, Eng>Backend, Eng>Frontend; Backend:Alice, Frontend:Bob, HR:Carol; Alice, Bob
Company>Eng, Eng>Backend; Backend:Alice, Backend:Dave; Alice, Dave
Company>Eng, Company>HR, Eng>Backend; Backend:Eve, HR:Eve, HR:Carol; Eve, Carol

hints: Build the group tree (parent -> children) and find the root (a group that never appears as a child). Also collect the set of groups each target employee directly belongs to.
Verify that every distinct target employee appears in memberships (if any is missing, return null). Deduplicate targetEmployees so you know the exact count k of distinct targets to cover.

Run a single post-order DFS (or bottom-up traversal with depth) from the root: each node computes the BitSet or Set of target employee indices present in its subtree (its own direct target employees union its children's sets). Any group covering all k targets is a valid candidate; pick the one with greatest depth (breaking ties lexicographically). Intended complexity: O((G + E) * k) (O(n) for fixed target count k), O(G + E) space.
inputSyntax: Input: parent>child, ...; group:emp, ...; target1, target2, for example: Company>Eng, Company>HR, Eng>Backend, Eng>Frontend; Backend:Alice, Frontend:Bob; Alice, Bob
sampleInput: Company>Eng, Company>HR, Eng>Backend, Eng>Frontend; Backend:Alice, Frontend:Bob; Alice, Bob
